items.title: Surviving the Antarctic: thermal tolerance adjustment in an invasive population of Psychoda albipennis (Zetterstedt, 1850)
items.abstract: Biological invasions in polar ecosystems are an increasing concern under climate change and intensifying human activity. We compared two geographically distant populations of the invasive dipteran Psychoda albipennis (Maritime Antarctica and the Magellanic sub-Antarctic) to assess population-level variation in lower and upper thermal tolerance. We further contextualized these responses through an exploratory comparison with published thermal-tolerance data for the non-native Trichocera maculipennis and the native Parochlus steinenii . Thermal responses in P. albipennis were asymmetric: responses to cooling were largely conserved between populations, whereas upper thermal tolerance diverged markedly, with the Antarctic population exhibiting a higher CT max and a slower decline in activity as temperature increased. In the exploratory interspecific comparison, all three species showed broadly similar responses to cooling, whereas P. albipennis and T. maculipennis exhibited higher upper thermal thresholds than P. steinenii . Together, these findings identify upper thermal tolerance as the primary axis of phenotypic thermal differentiation between P. albipennis populations. The broader functional thermal breadth observed in the Antarctic population may enhance persistence under thermally variable conditions, although the relative contributions of phenotypic plasticity, environmental filtering, and heritable evolutionary change remain unresolved.

items.title: Distance from the climatic niche optimum explains climate‐change‐driven dynamics in Mediterranean shrublands
items.abstract: Understanding vegetation responses to climatic variability is essential for anticipating future trajectories and informing management and conservation. Climatic niche metrics can improve climatic impact assessments by accounting for species‐specific climatic requirements. We analysed vegetation responses to gradual changes in climatic conditions in the monte blanco shrubland of Doñana National Park (SW Spain), one of Europe's most biodiverse protected areas. Specifically, we assessed vegetation dynamics over a 15‐year period (2007–2022) following a drought‐induced canopy loss event. We used species' climatic niche centroids as a proxy for their climatic optima and quantified their distance to observed climatic conditions as an indicator of climatic disequilibrium. We then examined temporal trends in centroid distance at community and species levels and tested their association with changes in shrub cover and community composition. Climatic conditions progressively shifted toward greater aridity during the study period, increasing centroid distance for all species but at different rates. Moreover, species‐specific rates of increase in centroid distance were associated with changes in shrub cover, although these changes mainly involved two of the ten species studied. The former dominant Halimium halimifolium, initially with the lowest centroid distance but experiencing the largest increase through time, declined in cover. By contrast, Salvia rosmarinus , which showed the highest initial centroid distance but a smaller increase, expanded. Consequently, community composition shifted, with H. halimifolium largely replaced by S. rosmarinus , while other species remained relatively stable. Although total shrub cover increased over the study period, it did not recover pre‐drought levels. Synthesis and applications . Assessing temporal changes in climatic disequilibrium can improve our understanding of vegetation dynamics under climate change. In Doñana shrublands, this approach helped explain contrasting species responses to gradual aridification, suggesting partial adaptation of community composition to emerging climatic conditions without overall cover loss. These assessments can inform conservation and adaptation planning by identifying potentially vulnerable taxa where vegetation data are limited and indicating whether community reorganization reflects adaptation to changing climatic conditions. By reliying on publicly available data, this approach offers a practical tool for assessing climatic impacts and management across terrestrial ecosystems worldwide.

items.title: Partitioning the variance of species–area relation into sampling‐ versus scale‐dependent components
items.abstract: The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample. We establish this decomposition mathematically and evaluate its behavior through numerical simulations. On this basis, empirical SAR observations can be classified as falling within the conditional confidence interval (CI), within the gap between the conditional and unconditional CIs, or outside the unconditional CI. The last outcome indicates variation not accounted for by the two sampling‐dependent components and may reflect scale‐dependent ecological processes or other sources of unexplained variation. Empirical applications showed that the relative contributions of local sampling uncertainty, regional richness uncertainty, and variation beyond these sampling‐dependent components differed among datasets, spatial scales, and sampling designs. For spatially explicit sampling of a tropical forest plot stem‐mapping dataset, observations were generally consistent with local sampling uncertainty when small sampling grains were freely distributed across space. In contrast, observations from a single contiguous sampling area more frequently fell outside the unconditional CI, a pattern that may reflect spatially structured ecological processes not represented by the sampling‐variance components. For nested sampling of amphibian diversity on the Chengdu Plain in SW China, both local sampling uncertainty and variation beyond the unconditional CI were frequently observed, whereas uncertainty in regional richness became more prominent when the local sampling area fraction exceeded 0.6. The resulting classifications also varied with the order of nested sampling: for the amphibian dataset, the large‐to‐small scheme accumulated species richness more slowly than the small‐to‐large scheme did. In conclusion, we develop a novel and readily applicable hierarchical variance‐partitioning framework to distinguish variation attributable to local sampling, uncertainty in regional richness, and variation not explained by these sampling‐dependent components along SAR curves.

items.title: Synergistic mechanistic and deep learning approaches for modeling insect thermal responses and geographic distributions
items.abstract: Aim The Hutchinsonian shortfall, the lack of knowledge about species' abiotic tolerance, limits our understanding of species responses to environmental change and consequently also the outlining of their distribution in space and time. Such environmental tolerance is commonly inferred with two distinct approaches: i) trait performance studies, which use lab experiments to model species' functional responses, often overlooking real-world complexity, and ii) species distribution models, which infer environmental suitability from occurrence data, but offer limited causal insights. In this paper, we argue that these two strategies bring complementary information that can be integrated to estimate species-environment relationships more robustly and accurately map species distributions. Location Global scale Time period 2000-2019 Major taxa studied Given their exceptional diversity and climatic sensitivity, insects provide a powerful system for studying these responses. We selected key insect species representing i) disease vectors: the yellow fever (Aedes aegypti) and Asian tiger (Aedes albopictus) mosquitoes; ii) agricultural pests: the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) and the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda); and iii) biocontrol agents: the green lacewing (Chrysoperla carnea) and the 14-spotted ladybug (Propylea quatuordecimpunctata). Methods We compared predicted insect thermal suitability and distributions derived from two complementary methodological approaches: mechanistic models based on experimentally derived thermal responses of ecological rates, and deep learning-based species distribution models based on occurrence data. We further tested hybrid frameworks integrating mechanistic and correlational information through model ensembling, mechanistic regularization, and mechanistically informed deep learning. We assessed the efficacy of these methods under increasing data scarcity by progressively removing up to 80% of species occurrence records using three strategies: removal from the warmest or coldest parts of species' thermal ranges, removal from the least-sampled locations based on geographic sampling bias, and random removal as a baseline. Results Our findings highlight that occurrence-derived thermal suitability closely reproduces the observed distributions of insects. Compared to the mechanistic estimates, these thermal response curves are consistently shifted towards lower temperatures, potentially reflecting niche underfilling. However, when challenged with progressive data removal, correlative methods fail to extrapolate reliably in data-deficient regimes, where mechanistic knowledge becomes increasingly more crucial. Hybrid approaches in turn leveraged complementary information, improving predictive performance and reducing the sensitivity of environmental suitability estimates to sampling biases. Main conclusions Ultimately, we show how the synergistic integration of experimental ecology with observational biogeography can lead to more accurate and ecologically robust predictions for species distributions and their environmental responses to climatic changes.

items.title: Traits and Evolutionary History Influence Community Structure in Snakes Across the World's Largest Savanna–Forest Ecotone
items.abstract: Aim We tested whether snake assemblages across the Amazonia–Cerrado ecotone are structured primarily by contemporary climatic gradients, geographic distance, or biome‐specific lineage turnover. We evaluated how taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional dimensions of biodiversity respond across the world's largest forest–savanna transition. Location Amazonia–Cerrado ecotone, South America. Taxon Snakes. Methods We compiled 67 snake assemblages representing 222 species across Amazonia, the Cerrado and their transition zone. We quantified taxonomic richness, phylogenetic species variability, functional richness, and taxonomic, phylogenetic, and functional β‐diversity. We evaluated sensitivity to phylogenetic uncertainty across 1000 phylogenies independently completed using Taxonomic Addition for Complete Trees (TACT). We used Bayesian models fitted with Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to assess environmental and spatial predictors of α‐diversity and generalized dissimilarity models (GDMs) to evaluate predictors of compositional dissimilarity and turnover. Results α‐diversity responses differed among biodiversity dimensions. Observed species richness decreased with increasing mean diurnal temperature range, whereas phylogenetic diversity showed a modest positive association with mean temperature during the wettest quarter. Functional richness showed no supported climatic or spatial associations. Phylogenetic α‐ and β‐diversity estimates were highly robust to stochastic phylogenetic completion. Across taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional dimensions, turnover generally exceeded nestedness. Biome identity was the dominant predictor of compositional dissimilarity. Pairwise geographic distance added little deviance overall, although it was supported for functional turnover; individual climatic predictors were generally weak. Taxonomic and functional turnover were pronounced despite comparatively limited differentiation among deep phylogenetic lineages. Main Conclusions Snake assemblages across the Amazonia–Cerrado ecotone are structured primarily by turnover of species and ecological strategies within dominant Neotropical radiations rather than by replacement among deeply divergent evolutionary lineages. Biome‐scale ecological and historical differences more strongly influence assemblage differentiation than isolated contemporary climatic gradients. Local functional richness showed no supported centroid‐distance pattern, whereas functional composition changed strongly between biomes and showed a modest independent distance‐decay component. These results highlight the importance of integrating taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional dimensions to understand how biome transitions organize biodiversity across space.

items.title: Large‐Scale Biogeographic Structuring of Pacific Abyssal Communities Revealed by eDNA Metabarcoding
items.abstract: Aim At depths between 3000 and 6000 m, abyssal plains comprise over half of Earth's surface yet remain among the least biologically characterised ocean regions, particularly in the central Pacific where remoteness has constrained understanding of biodiversity and biogeography. Here, we apply environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding across abyssal sites between Mexico, Hawai‘i and Tahitī spanning > 5700 km to investigate broad‐scale biogeographic structuring and characterise biodiversity patterns. Location Abyssal Pacific Ocean. Methods We applied two fish‐targeted assays (MiFish‐U and 16S Fish) and one broad metazoan assay (COI Leray) to 252 eDNA samples collected from 4289 to 5666 m using near‐bottom Niskin water sampling and passive substrates (filter papers and polyurethane foam). Results Across the transects, 256 species spanning 123 families and 14 metazoan phyla were identified. Community composition differed between transects and among sites, revealing spatial structuring at regional and local scales. These patterns were supported by significant distance‐decay relationships, although strength varied among assays. Community differences were overwhelmingly driven by taxonomic turnover rather than nestedness, indicating abyssal assemblages comprise distinct regional communities rather than nested subsets of a cosmopolitan fauna. This structuring was associated with geographic position and environmental gradients, including depth and bottom‐water properties, indicating that community composition is structured by basin‐scale gradients and local habitat variation across the sampled transects. Sampling method influenced biodiversity detection but did not override spatial patterns, with active and passive approaches capturing complementary components of the community. Main Conclusions Across more than 5700 km of the Pacific abyssal plain, biodiversity was structured across multiple spatial scales rather than being homogeneous. eDNA resolves both basin‐scale biogeographic patterns and site‐level ecological variation, revealing how biodiversity is organised across a vast and under‐characterised biome. By capturing biodiversity largely inaccessible to conventional sampling, eDNA provides a powerful approach for resolving the distribution and organisation of life in Earth's largest biome.

items.title: Identifying key biodiversity areas in Mozambique for conservation planning and policy
items.abstract: The world is experiencing unprecedented rates of biodiversity loss. To reverse this trend, signatories to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) have committed to conserving at least 30% of marine and terrestrial areas by 2030, with an emphasis on sites critical for biodiversity. One mechanism to support this goal is the identification of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) to inform spatial planning and the development of conservation area networks. However, few case studies demonstrate how the KBA process can be implemented in high-biodiversity, low-income countries. We present a national-scale example from Mozambique, where KBAs were delineated across seven taxonomic groups, and outline a post hoc theory of change to support broader national implementation and progress towards CBD targets. We describe how the project established institutional arrangements and training to build technical capacity, highlighting the central role of the Ministry of Land and Environment. We then present the KBA identification process and results, including species Red List assessments that contributed to the identification of four marine and 25 terrestrial KBAs. With results integrated into national policy and legislation, the Mozambique KBA system demonstrates that KBA identification is feasible in lower-income countries and provides a model for broader application.

items.title: Climatic Niche‐Based Identification of In‐Situ Climate Refugia to Support China's Conservation Planning Toward the 30 × 30 Target
items.abstract: Aim Climate change increasingly threatens biodiversity by altering habitat conditions and undermining the long‐term effectiveness of protected area (PA) networks. In situ climate refugia—locations that retain relatively stable climatic conditions—are essential for supporting species persistence under future climate scenarios and for meeting global conservation targets such as “30 × 30.” This study aims to identify in situ climate refugia across China using a climatic niche–based framework and to assess the degree to which these refugia are represented within the existing PA network. Location Mainland China. Time Period Baseline (1970–2000) and future projections for 2081–2100 under SSP2‐4.5 and SSP5‐8.5 scenarios Major Taxa Studied 282 endangered terrestrial vertebrates, including 68 mammals, 153 amphibians, 35 reptiles, and 26 non‐migratory birds. Methods We developed a climatic niche–based framework that integrates species‐specific climatic tolerances, climate change intensity, and habitat suitability to identify potential climate refugia at a national scale. Unlike traditional approaches reliant on broad, species‐neutral climate stability thresholds, our method uses species‐specific climatic niche widths (CNWs) to derive ecologically grounded climatic tolerance thresholds, enabling more species‐informed identification of refugial areas. Results Approximately 23% of mainland China's land area was classified as high‐potential climate refugia, concentrated mainly in the subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest and tropical monsoon rainforest. However, only 15% of these areas currently fall within PAs. Incorporating high‐potential refugia alone could increase national PA coverage from 19% to 38%, while adding medium‐potential refugia could raise overall protection to 56%. Main Conclusions Species‐specific CNWs provide a realistic and ecologically informed basis for delimiting refugia under climate change. The pronounced mismatch between identified climate refugia and China's existing PA network highlights critical conservation gaps, especially within subtropical and tropical biomes. High‐ and medium‐potential refugia identify opportunities for further ecological assessment and protection planning toward the 30 × 30 target. The proposed framework is scalable and applicable to other regions seeking to incorporate climate‐adaptive principles into systematic conservation planning.

items.title: Ecological Processes Shape Species Diversity and Distributions in a Trans‐Tasman Velvet Worm Genus
items.abstract: Aim Studies on the geographic distributions of terrestrial invertebrates with Gondwanan legacies have often focused on historical biogeography without considering ecological processes. Here, we focus on species diversity and distributional patterns of the trans‐Tasman egg‐laying velvet worm genus Ooperipatellus and investigate how climatic niches and refugia have shaped the present‐day distributions seen in this group. Location Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand. Taxon Velvet worm genus Ooperipatellus (Onychophora, Peripatopsidae). Methods We combined ultraconserved element (UCE) data and species delimitation with divergence dating and climatic niche analyses to explore the role of climate change in shaping present‐day species diversity and distributions. Results Our genomic data provide evidence for six putative new species of Ooperipatellus in Aotearoa New Zealand. We also show that the two main Ooperipatellus clades, AUS and NZ, occupy largely different environmental conditions, partly because the NZ niche lies in climates absent from Australia today. Occupied environmental space is more partitioned among Australian species than among New Zealand species, which show greater overlap. This is in contrast to geographic range overlap, which appears greater in Tasmania than in New Zealand. Niche models indicate that suitable environment for Ooperipatellus on the mainland of Australia has contracted since the Last Glacial Maximum, with species today currently occupying climate refugia. This analysis also reveals the presence of historical refugia in northwestern Tasmania which we hypothesize may have contributed to the east–west biodiversity patterns documented on the island. Most divergences among NZ Ooperipatellus species postdate the onset of the uplift of Kā Tiritiri o te Moana (the Southern Alps). One such divergence highlights a phylogeographic relationship across the southern Alpine Fault, this pattern is also replicated in other, distantly related taxa. Main Conclusions Our exploration of biogeographic patterns in this genus of rare saproxylic invertebrates underscores the dynamic interplay of organism, climate and geography in shaping taxon distributions and generating and maintaining diversity. The two main Ooperipatellus clades differ in the environmental conditions they occupy and in how they partition environmental and geographic space. The putative role of climatic refugia in shaping the distributions of these animals highlights the evolutionary complexity and contemporary vulnerability of these species.

items.title: Climate Change and Habitat Loss Threaten Taxonomic and Functional Diversity of Endemic Primates in South America
items.abstract: Aim To assess impacts of climate change and forest cover on taxonomic and functional diversity of endemic and threatened primates in South America. Location South America. Taxon Endemic and threatened primates. Methods We modelled climatic suitability for 68 taxa using consensus species distribution models for a baseline period (1981–2010) and two future periods (2041–2070; 2071–2100), under an intermediate (SSP3‐7.0) and a high‐end (SSP5‐8.5) emission scenario. The projections incorporated dispersal constraints and were combined with forest cover scenarios. Taxonomic diversity was estimated as species richness, whereas functional diversity was quantified as mean pairwise distance (MPD), which represents the average functional dissimilarity among co‐occurring taxa based on body mass, activity pattern, habitat, and trophic guild, at a 5 km resolution. The spatial congruence between taxonomic and functional diversity was assessed using geographically weighted correlation and generalized additive models. Results Most taxa showed a significant contraction of suitable range, especially under the most severe scenario (SSP5‐8.5 in 2071–2100), when more than half were projected to lose > 50% of their distribution. Areas of higher taxonomic and functional diversity were projected to contract in the Amazon and the Atlantic Forest, persisting mainly in the southwestern Amazon and the Magdalena River region. Under this scenario, taxa projected to lose more than 50% of their suitable area represented 23.3% of the summed functional distinctiveness of the 178‐taxon primate pool. The congruence between taxonomic and functional diversity increases in future projections, reflecting a concentration of species and functions in climatically more stable areas. Main Conclusions Climate change associated with forest loss may promote taxonomic erosion and functional simplification of primate communities. The projected increase in congruence may reflect environmental filtering and concentration in potential refugia, rather than ecological stability. Conservation strategies should incorporate functional metrics and prioritize areas that maintain functionally distinct taxa, as well as overall diversity.

items.title: deepSTRAPP: An R package to assess trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification dynamics over time
items.abstract: Understanding how diversification dynamics interact with species traits and geographical distributions over time remains a central challenge in macroevolution and biogeography. Yet the timing of these associations is rarely tested explicitly: existing approaches often focus on present‐day trait–rate relationships, or summarize over the whole history of a clade, overlooking variations in historical processes acting over deep evolutionary timescales. We introduce deepSTRAPP , an R package for assessing trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification across any temporal interval. deepSTRAPP models the evolution of traits or ranges independently of diversification rates on time‐calibrated phylogenies, extracts inferred values at user‐defined time steps and performs semi‐parametric STRAPP (Structured Rate Permutations on Phylogenies) tests based on block‐permutation to identify time windows in which diversification rates varied with species attributes. It handles continuous, categorical and biogeographic data, and includes visualization tools to explore the evolution of traits, ranges, diversification rates and the significance of their associations through time. Applied to empirical datasets, deepSTRAPP provided critical new perspectives to macroevolutionary questions inaccessible to currently available methods. It uncovered significant state‐dependent dynamics confined to restricted time windows that whole‐tree analyses overlooked, and tempered conclusions about present‐day associations that did not extend substantially back through evolutionary time. By explicitly testing for temporal variation in trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification, deepSTRAPP provides a robust framework to disentangle the relative contributions of past versus recent processes in shaping biodiversity patterns across broad phylogenetic and temporal scales.

items.title: The Filtering Effects of Urban Environments on Frugivorous Birds Worldwide
items.abstract: Aim Frugivorous birds are highly susceptible to environmental changes caused by urbanization. However, little is known about the global consequences. Here, we examine global patterns of urban frugivorous bird diversity and the mechanisms driving these patterns. Location Global, across 1414 urban areas. Time Period Contemporary. Major Taxa Studied Frugivorous birds. Methods After compiling a global dataset of urban bird assemblages, we compared the species richness and composition of frugivorous birds in urban areas with those of their regional species pools derived from BirdLife range maps and partitioned the composition dissimilarity into its spatial turnover and nestedness components. We assessed how climatic, ecological, socio‐economic, and biogeographic factors accounted for variation in the species richness of urban frugivorous birds. Results We identified 557 frugivorous bird species in these urban areas. Variations in the species richness among urban areas were significantly associated with temperature, historical biogeography, habitat heterogeneity, socio‐economic conditions, and the diversity of fleshy‐fruited trees. Globally, the total number of frugivorous bird species in urban areas was 33.9% lower than in the combined regional species pools. Individually, 531 urban areas exhibited lower frugivorous richness, 329 matched their regional levels, and 554 had higher frugivorous richness than their regional species pools. These declines were more pervasive in tropical regions, where ca. 91.8% of urban areas contained fewer frugivorous species. The compositional dissimilarity between urban assemblages and their regional species pools was dominated by nestedness, regardless of whether the urban areas gained or lost species. Main Conclusions Our results highlight the strong filtering effects of urbanization on frugivorous birds. These insights can inform strategies for conserving frugivores in cities.

items.title: Blueprints for restoration: Molecular monitoring and remote sensing support dispersal‐driven kelp recolonization
items.abstract: Nearshore marine habitats generate services worth billions of dollars, yet they are undergoing rapid, widespread degradation worldwide. Along northern California's coastline, a key habitat-forming annual species, bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana), has experienced historic declines of up to 95%. These losses have prompted efforts to uncover the mechanisms that influence kelp forest recovery, with the goal of restoring degraded habitats. Zoospore dispersal between neighboring populations is thought to be a key driver of recovery, yet the degree to which spore supply limits recolonization remains unresolved. A long-standing debate centers on whether persistent "gametophyte banks" fuel post-disturbance regrowth or whether recovery depends primarily on newly settled zoospores. To address this question, we combined high-resolution PlanetScope satellite imagery with molecular quantification of kelp gametophyte densities to assess how habitat connectivity influences recolonization. Connectivity to extant kelp in 2023 was a significant predictor of gametophyte density, kelp canopy occurrence, and habitat recolonization in 2024, suggesting that dispersal plays an important role in recolonization. By linking spatial connectivity with densities of microscopic life stages and recolonization, this work offers valuable guidance for designing and implementing effective kelp restoration strategies.

items.title: Active management strengthens recovery in China's freshwater protected areas
items.abstract: Research Highlight article about: Liang, Z., Rypel, A. L., Liu, J., & Guo, C. (2026). Targeted fish removals enhance multidimensional native fish diversity within freshwater protected areas. Journal of Applied Ecology, 63 , e70521, https://doi.org/10.1111/1365‐2664.70521 . Freshwater protected areas (FPAs) are increasingly used to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services, yet protection alone may not always deliver ecological recovery, particularly where non‐native species also benefit from reduced fishing pressure. Liang et al. (2026) address this challenge by comparing Chinese lake FPAs managed with and without targeted fish removals (TFRs). Their results indicate that recovery is multidimensional: combining FPAs with TFRs can enhance native fish diversity across taxonomic and functional dimensions while strengthening top‐down trophic regulation. Importantly, outcomes depend on which ecological guilds are targeted, highlighting the need for adaptive and functionally informed management rather than uniform removal strategies. Rather than treating protection as an endpoint, Liang et al. (2026) show that freshwater recovery may require protection to work hand in hand with active management.

items.title: Complex lake effects structure bryophyte communities across spatial scales around Lake Superior, Canada
items.abstract: Context Studies have found that large lakes significantly modify regional climates, an influence known as the “lake effect”. Large lakes may provide biodiversity refugia in a changing climate owing to the lake effect, but the impacts of lake effects on biodiversity remain poorly documented. Objectives We sought to quantify the influence of the lake effect on bryophyte communities in the vicinity of Lake Superior, and to disentangle the lake effect from processes occurring at larger (regional) and smaller (forest stand) scales. Methods We sampled bryophyte communities on three substrates (trees, rocks, and logs) across 54 sites on and near the northern and eastern shores of Lake Superior. We combined community data with climate and forest data to determine the influence of variables at each of three spatial scales—micro (forest attributes), meso (lake effect), and macro (regional climatic norms)—on community composition and richness. Results The lake effect structured community composition, along with regional climate norms and forest characteristics. The lake effect was divided into three orthogonal axes. Notably, each of these axes included a distinct component of the moisture environment—precipitation, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit—and our results suggest that these components have divergent effects on bryophyte communities. The lake effect had no significant influence on species richness. Conclusions Lake Superior induces biotically important climatic heterogeneity that structures bryophyte communities across the study region. The near-lake environment may be an important thermal and hydrologic refuge for bryophytes in a warming, drying climate.

items.title: Coupled MaxEnt-InVEST modelling identifies habitat suitability, quality and conservation gaps of Garrulax maximus
items.abstract: Introduction Habitat degradation and conservation gaps severely threaten China's endemic montane birds, yet few studies have integrated habitat suitability with quality assessment. Methods Using the nationally protected Giant Laughingthrush (Garrulax maximus) across five provinces in western China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we coupled optimized MaxEnt, InVEST, and GIS approaches to quantify potential distribution, habitat quality, conservation gaps, and environmental drivers. ResultsThe MaxEnt model performed robustly (mean AUC = 0.946). Climate dominated distribution (69.3% cumulative contribution), with annual precipitation (bio12, 35.7%) as the core limiting factor. The species occupied a cold-humid niche: annual precipitation 631.60–794.65 mm, driest-quarter temperature −7.12–2.75 °C, and elevation 2496.79–4012.78 m. High-suitability areas centered on the western Sichuan Basin rim, decreasing outward. Notably, a spatial mismatch emerged between habitat quality and suitability: Yunnan held the largest high-quality habitat (17.28 × 104 km2) but limited priority conservation areas, whereas Sichuan, with less high-quality habitat (13.63 × 104 km2), contained the largest priority zones (6.95 × 104 km2), indicating complementarity rather than substitution. Conservation gaps were extensive (54.26%–75.98%), mainly along reserve boundaries and buffers, revealing structural deficiencies from overemphasizing core zones while neglecting corridors. DiscussionThese findings underscore the urgency of reassessing and expanding protected area networks to cover priority zones. Our integrated framework offers a scientific reference for conserving the Giant Laughingthrush and managing montane birds within the Hengduan Mountains biodiversity hotspot, with implications for broader conservation planning in ecologically sensitive regions.

items.title: Beaver Impacts Tool: A Graphical User Interface for Analyzing Ecosystem Impacts of Beaver Dams Using Remote Sensing Data
items.abstract: Beavers are being increasingly recognized as driving factors in diverse and resilient riparian ecosystems. Many of their impacts, including changes to water levels and vegetation, can be studied through remote sensing. However, ecologists and conservationists may lack the tools to easily analyze remote sensing data for these purposes. We offer here a Google Earth Engine-backed Streamlit app that allows users to easily upload locations of observed dams or installed beaver dam analogs for analysis. Via a graphical user interface, users then generate a set of dam-absent locations for comparison and receive plots and numerical data indicating how indices associated with vegetation, water, temperature, and evapotranspiration change over time for dam-present and dam-absent locations. Based on the availability of open datasets, our tool provides coverage from 2017 onward. The cloud version of the tool can be accessed via a static URL, or users can run the app locally using code and documentation provided on github. We believe this tool will allow a wider range of ecologists and conservationists to complement their work with the use of remote sensing data, without the need to gain expertise in specific software.

items.title: Climate change drives northward range shifts in invasive forest pests and pathogens
items.abstract: Invasive tree pests and pathogens are increasingly threatening forests worldwide. Understanding how a warming climate and changing precipitation patterns will affect the future distribution ranges of these pathogenic species requires systematic analysis across a variety of host trees and pathogenic species. We analysed 31 major tree pests and pathogens that have caused widespread and extensive damage globally, predicting their current and future distribution under various climate change scenarios using species distribution modelling. Our results showed that tree pests and pathogens will consistently shift northward, threatening northern temperate and boreal forests between the years 2041 and 2080. On the other hand, some warmer regions, including southern Europe, were expected to experience fewer pest and pathogen outbreaks in the future. Annual mean temperature, mean temperature of the warmest quarter, precipitation of the warmest quarter, and precipitation of the driest month contributed to the species distribution models, indicating that warming temperatures and moderate precipitation may promote the survival, reproduction, and spread of the pathogenic agents. Our research highlights the need for enhanced monitoring, early pest and pathogen detection, stricter biosecurity measures, and improved silvicultural strategies in temperate and boreal forests in the northern hemisphere. Moreover, forest assessments, including those focused on carbon budgets, biodiversity, and ecosystem services, should account for the effects of tree pests and pathogen outbreaks, as they may drastically alter future functioning of forests globally.

items.title: Sacred natural sites in Pantanal and surrounding highlands: spatial overlap with ecological corridors and priority resilience climate change areas
items.abstract: Protected areas face increasing challenges due to climate change and land-use transformations, prompting the need for complementary conservation strategies such as sacred natural sites. Sacred natural sites, valued for their cultural and spiritual significance, historically harbor rich biodiversity and provide key ecosystem services. We investigate the distribution and conservation relevance of sacred natural sites in Pantanal lowlands and surrounding highlands plateau, the Cerrado, two biologically diverse regions that form the upper Paraguay River basin in Brazil. Based on the understanding that landscape features influence both ecological processes and cultural practices, we analyzed the spatial congruence between sacred natural sites, ecological corridors, and Priority Resilience Climate Change Areas. We found a significant spatial overlap between sacred natural sites and ecological corridors, indicating that sacred natural sites may contribute to biodiversity connectivity, especially at local scales, assuming they maintain habitat integrity and ecological conditions that support species movement. We found no statistically significant overlap between sacred natural sites and Priority Resilience Climate Change Areas, which likely reflects the spatial stationarity of high-resilience areas across the Pantanal, driven using wetland density as a key input in the resilience assessment. These results suggest that sacred natural sites can complement formal conservation strategies by serving both ecological and cultural functions. Recognizing and integrating sacred natural sites into frameworks such as “other effective area-based conservation measures” could enhance biodiversity protection while respecting community rights and spiritual values in a changing climate. The post Sacred natural sites in Pantanal and surrounding highlands: spatial overlap with ecological corridors and priority resilience climate change areas first appeared on Ecology & Society .

items.title: Assessing Strategies to Optimize Participatory Science Data in Species Distribution Models
items.abstract: Aims Data from participatory science projects are widely used to understand species distributions. However, participatory science data often contain biases that can obscure real patterns. We address two sources of sampling bias: location uncertainty of individual records and spatially heterogeneous sampling effort. A variety of data processing and modelling strategies have been used to address these biases, without consensus on their relative effectiveness. We test several strategies using data from iNaturalist, a large repository of participatory science data. Location Twenty‐four amphibian ranges of varying sizes and locations within the continental United States. Method We fit species distribution models with iNaturalist data for 24 amphibian species to compare the effectiveness of strategies intended to improve distribution estimates. We examined three categories of strategies: (1) filtering out records with high location uncertainty, (2) thinning to reduce heterogeneous effort, and (3) observation models that account for heterogeneous effort without removing data. We evaluated the predictive accuracy of each approach using validation data from systematic surveys with constant effort and known locations. Results The strategies we tested generally had little effect on predictive accuracy as measured by AUC, with no consistent pattern across species. Instead, we found that the minimal change in performance was influenced by the species‐specific search process, the distribution of records, and the resolution of the analysis. Main Conclusion None of the strategies we tested consistently improve model performance, but our results provide a foundation for a species‐ and analysis‐specific approach. Further improvement in model performance may require additional information or novel methods.

items.title: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
items.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we assessed whether squamate reptiles inside PAs experience lower heat exposure than conspecifics in unprotected, human‐modified landscapes, and how this buffering effect varies across latitudes, biomes, and evolutionary lineages. Using biophysical modelling of operative temperatures across 248 species, we show that PAs consistently reduced both annual hours above critical thermal maximum (CT max ) and the frequency of critical days under current and future climatic scenarios (+2°C and + 4°C). We found that under current climate, protected sites had 51 fewer hours above CT max and 3.5 fewer critical days than unprotected sites, and the proportional reduction persisted under +2°C and + 4°C warming scenarios. The buffering effect was most pronounced at low latitudes and tropical biomes, where species already operate close to their thermal limits. Deserts and xeric shrublands, together with tropical grasslands and savannas, emerged as biomes with elevated heat exposure, reinforcing growing concern for arid‐zone reptiles under climate change. Substantial phylogenetic signal in heat exposure indicated that evolutionary history shapes thermal vulnerability beyond geography and biome alone, with the magnitude of PA buffering varying considerably across squamate lineages. Our findings demonstrate that PAs can provide refugia from heat exposure, and that their conservation value under climate change depends on the retention of structurally complex habitats and thermally heterogeneous microhabitats.

items.title: Climate‐driven compositional shifts across a temperate–subtropical island ecotone
items.abstract: Climate change is expected to drive substantial shifts in species distributions, yet ecological responses are often delayed under disequilibrium dynamics, limiting the effectiveness of range‐based indicators for detecting ongoing change. Compositional approaches have been proposed as an alternative; however, conventional comparisons based on gradient shape or pointwise differences may fail to detect change when the overall gradient structure is conserved, because small and spatially heterogeneous differences cancel out across the gradient. Here, we address this limitation by presenting a direction‐sensitive analytical framework that integrates signed differences along environmental gradients. Using a comprehensive dataset of island floras across a temperate–subtropical transition in South Korea, we quantify temporal changes in the relative representation of warm‐temperate and subtropical plant (WTSP) assemblages. By emphasizing proportional changes along latitudinal gradients, we detect directional redistribution within communities even in the absence of pronounced changes in gradient shape. Our results reveal patterns consistent with northward redistribution of WTSP composition across survey periods, despite minimal changes in overall gradient form, indicating that community‐level redistribution can occur prior to detectable range shifts or richness changes. These findings highlight the sensitivity of cumulative, direction‐sensitive compositional metrics for detecting early ecological responses to climate warming. More broadly, this study provides a generalizable framework for detecting compositional redistribution through cumulative inference, even when conventional approaches may have limited sensitivity under some conditions, and for identifying early signals of climate‐driven change across gradient‐structured ecological systems. Transitional systems may therefore serve as particularly sensitive contexts for detecting incipient biogeographical change under ongoing warming.

items.title: Migrant frugivorous birds assist plants in tracking climate change: A first spatially explicit approach
items.abstract: Climate change is causing biodiversity redistributions towards cooler areas at an unprecedented velocity. Plants are an essential component of terrestrial ecosystems that primarily rely on seed dispersal to redistribute. Yet, most seed dispersal occurs over short distances (i.e. less than 1 km), which is insufficient to track ongoing climate change. Bird migration can support seed dispersal at longer distances. However, we lack spatially explicit estimations of seed dispersal by migratory birds towards future climatically suitable ranges of plants. Thereby, it remains unclear to what extent they can facilitate plant redistribution in the coming decades. We integrated spatially explicit, seed‐dispersal models with projections on plant climatic suitability using species distribution models. We simulated long‐distance dispersal of 14 fleshy‐fruited plant species across Europe during the northward spring migration of song thrushes ( Turdus philomelos ), an adequate model species given its abundance, migratory behaviour and key role as disperser of native European plants. Dispersal models were replicated under three global warming projections and three scenarios of dispersal sensitivity to land‐cover alteration. Plant climatically suitable ranges will shift northwards by 248–948 km under severe warming projections by the year 2090. We identified a strong negative effect of warmer climate projections and higher dispersal sensitivity to land‐cover alteration on seed‐dispersal range filling (i.e. the proportion of future climatically suitable area that is currently unsuitable and receives seed‐dispersal events). Seed‐dispersal range filling averaged 22.2% across species under severe warming and assuming no sensitivity to land‐cover alteration. We found substantial interspecific variation in seed‐dispersal range filling, which was higher in species with lesser changes in their potential ranges and with smaller seeds dispersed over longer distances. Synthesis . Migrant frugivorous birds can partially assist fleshy‐fruited plants fruiting during spring migration to track climate change, although severe warming and land‐cover alteration may strongly constrain seed‐dispersal range filling. Importantly, range filling capacity is uneven across plant species: differences in climatically suitable ranges and intrinsic traits, particularly seed size, influence the ability of species to reach newly suitable areas. Interspecific variation in plant capacity to redistribute could be crucial for the reassembly of ecological communities under climate change.

items.title: Multidimensional β diversity reveals the interplay of dispersal limitation and ecological filtering in structuring land‐bridge island butterfly communities
items.abstract: The theory of island biogeography (TIB) explains species richness patterns, yet its extension to compositional dissimilarity (β diversity), particularly from multidimensional perspectives, remains limited. Using butterfly assemblages across 44 land‐bridge islands in the Zhoushan Archipelago, China, we applied an integrative framework to unravel how island geography and species traits shape multi‐faceted β diversity. We partitioned taxonomic, phylogenetic, and functional β diversity into turnover and nestedness components, quantified species and site contributions, and distinguished roles of widespread versus restricted species. Key findings reveal: 1) dimensionality‐specific geographic drivers: inter‐island isolation differences primarily influenced nestedness in taxonomic and phylogenetic dimensions, suggesting its role as a filter for ordered species loss. In contrast, island area differences consistently affected both turnover and nestedness across all dimensions, underscoring its role as a master filter of resources and habitat. Island geographic attributes (e.g. isolation) only explained local community uniqueness in the taxonomic dimension. 2) A trait‐mediated mechanism: species with weaker dispersal capacity (smaller thorax area) contributed more to β diversity (higher species contribution), providing direct trait‐based evidence for dispersal limitation. 3) Internal metacommunity structure: nestedness was predominantly structured by widespread species, whereas turnover was driven mainly by the idiosyncratic distributions of restricted species. Our study demonstrates that island community assembly emerges from deterministic filtering (area and isolation shaping the widespread species backbone) interacting with stochastic processes (governing restricted species). This integrates TIB with β diversity by showing that TIB's core predictors (area and isolation) differentially shape the components of β diversity and offers a multidimensional, mechanistic framework for island conservation that emphasizes protecting island networks, source islands, and unique species and habitats.

items.title: Root biomass fraction of forest-planted sugar maple seedlings varies with climate of population origin across a latitudinal gradient
items.abstract: Planting seedlings beyond a species’ or population’s current distribution is a potential management strategy to help plants keep pace with changing climate. The extent to which both climate of origin and spatial climate differences affect seedling traits such as biomass allocation, however, remains poorly understood. Sugar maple ( Acer saccharum ) seedlings from three USA source populations with contrasting climates (from south to north; Missouri, Iowa, Minnesota) were grown for three years at nine forested sites, from Arkansas, USA, to Ontario, Canada, to test hypotheses about ecotypic and biogeographic variation in root biomass fraction (RMF, assessed herein with root biomass/[root biomass + stem biomass]). Sites spanned the north-south transect of the species’ range and extended beyond both northern and southern range margins. Our two main predictions were (i) seedling RMF would increase from southern to northern sites as a reflection of increasing resource constraints, and (ii) for similar reasons, seedlings with origins from further north would on average have both greater RMF and less plasticity in RMF than seedlings from further south. In contrast to our predictions, southern-origin seedlings overall had higher RMF than northern-origin seedlings, with central-origin seedlings intermediate. Southern-origin seedlings had greater RMF at northern than at southern sites, as predicted, but northern and central-origin seedlings did not. Determining how belowground allocation and its plasticity vary across populations and naturally existing biogeographic gradients offers a window into how species may respond to ongoing climate change.

items.title: Latitudinal Phylogenetic and Diversity Gradients Are Explained by a Tropical‐Temperate Transitional Bioregion
items.abstract: Aim To investigate how large‐scale ecological and evolutionary processes shape biodiversity patterns, with a focus on understanding the origins of latitudinal phylogenetic and diversity gradients. We emphasize the importance of accurately delineating bioregions to reveal the underlying evolutionary structure of biodiversity. Location Global, with emphasis on transitions between tropical and temperate bioregions. Time Period Contemporary distributions, analysed in the context of deep evolutionary histories. Major Taxa Studied Woody angiosperm tree species. Methods We compiled a comprehensive dataset of global tree species distributions and phylogenetic relationships. Using a data‐driven clustering approach, we delineated phyloregions: bioregions based on shared evolutionary history. We further applied simulation models to test whether the presence of transitional regions influences the emergence of latitudinal gradients. Results We identified a previously unrecognized transitional zone between tropical and temperate bioregions, termed the “bridge” phyloregion. This phyloregion is characterized by a distinct evolutionary composition and a weaker association with climatic and environmental parameters compared with adjacent phyloregions. Simulation models demonstrate that the latitudinal diversity and phylogenetic gradients are much more likely to emerge when such a transitional phyloregion exists. This finding supports the interpretation of the bridge phyloregion as a stepping‐stone facilitating colonization of species between contrasting climatic zones. Main Conclusions Our findings reveal that accurate delineation of evolutionary bioregions (phyloregions) uncovers previously hidden structures, including a bridge phyloregion with fundamental evolutionary roles. Recognizing these cryptic phyloregions provides new insights into the processes leading to large‐scale patterning of biodiversity.

items.title: Thermal baselines and climate‐space geometry mediate systematic terrestrial biodiversity responses to warming
items.abstract: Global warming is rapidly restructuring biological communities, yet terrestrial ecosystems often appear to lack the systematic climate‐driven signatures observed in marine realms. We hypothesise that this apparent idiosyncrasy arises from neglecting the geographic structure of climate. Using 1161 terrestrial community time series, we transitioned from geographic grids to a multidimensional climate space defined by temperature and precipitation. This framework allows climatic associations to be evaluated while accounting for climate‐space geometry by quantifying two key components: climate area and climate isolation. Using Bayesian hierarchical models, we evaluated how baseline climate and climate‐space geometry jointly shape temporal trends in richness, abundance, and evenness. While the average effect of warming on biodiversity appeared non‐significant, we found that terrestrial biodiversity responses varied systematically with baseline climate and climate‐space geometry. Species richness increased with warming in cooler climates but declined in the warmest regions. Furthermore, richness responses to warming became more positive in climatic regimes occupying larger areas, while the evenness response to warming depended on the interaction between climate area and isolation. Our findings identify the geography of climate as a critical link for understanding terrestrial biodiversity shifts. By treating climate as both an environmental condition and a spatial structure, we reveal coherent community responses to warming that were previously obscured in geographic space. These results suggest that conservation strategies benefit from looking beyond local temperature rates to consider the extent and connectivity of the climatic regimes being reshaped by climate change.

items.title: Elephants reshape woody vegetation dynamics in southern African savannas at local and landscape scales
items.abstract: Elephants and other megaherbivores can strongly modify woody vegetation, yet their influence across heterogeneous landscapes and spatial scales remains poorly resolved. Here, we combined remotely sensed time series of vegetation height (2000–2022) and woody cover (2015–2025) with elephant population counts from 34 reserves across eight southern African countries to investigate the relationship between elephants and woody vegetation dynamics at local and landscape scales. To represent uneven within‐reserve use, we further used movement data from 315 GPS‐collared elephants to model habitat selection and estimate spatially explicit local densities in 15 reserves. Across reserves, vegetation height generally decreased whereas woody cover generally increased. Both trends varied nonlinearly with reserve‐average elephant density: reserves with 1–2 elephants km −2 experienced the fastest declines in height and increases in cover, whereas increases in woody cover were weak or absent at the highest observed densities (approximately three elephants km −2 ), although uncertainty was substantial. At the local scale (1 km 2 ), vegetation dynamics were most strongly linked to fire frequency and changes in rainfall, yet higher estimated elephant density was associated with faster declines in vegetation height and progressively weaker gains in woody cover; the fitted woody‐cover trend became negative at the highest local densities (≥ 4 elephants km −2 ). These results indicate that elephants, at sufficient densities, can slow down increases in woody cover and promote shifts toward shorter vegetation locally, but have less pronounced effects at the reserve scale. The latter may reflect low population densities or a balance between positive (seed dispersal, resprouting) and negative (browsing, stem breakage) impacts on woody vegetation. Overall, our findings show that elephants can maintain open savanna structure where densities, or local concentrations of landscape use, are sufficiently high, emphasizing the importance of protecting and restoring viable populations.

items.title: Priority–green island synergy: A testable hypothesis for insect-mediated invasional facilitation in Eucalyptus plantations
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 113-121 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.207941 Authors: Xiu Xu, Zhende Yang Abstract: Non-native forest plantations can concentrate susceptible hosts, recurrently receive alien organisms through movements of planting material and thereby become focal points for biological invasions. Yet, whether an alien insect can directly alter host tissues in ways that facilitate a later alien insect remains poorly understood. We propose priority–green island synergy as a testable hypothesis for insect-mediated invasional facilitation. In southern China, the earlier-detected gall inducer Leptocybe invasa and the later-detected leaf gallers Ophelimus bipolaris and O. maskelli provide a candidate system. Leptocybe invasa galls alter nutrient, phenolic and phytohormone profiles and may generate transient physiological islands in galled or connected tissues. The hypothesis predicts that, after host genotype, tissue age, microclimate and propagule pressure are controlled, prior L. invasa attack should increase Ophelimus host acceptance, gall initiation or survival; that any benefit should co-vary with measurable physiological traits; that locally mediated effects should decline with increasing distance from the primary L. invasa gall; that the direction and magnitude of the response should vary with primary gall density and the interval between primary and secondary attack; and that any facilitative response should co-vary with realised gall development and associated physiological changes. Taken together, these predictions are designed to distinguish gall-mediated facilitation from alternative explanations for co-occurrence, including shared host susceptibility, propagule pressure, environmental filtering and variation in local adult abundance. We outline matched field surveys, controlled arrival-order experiments and physiological mediation tests that can evaluate the hypothesis and distinguish facilitation from alternative explanations. If supported, priority–green island synergy would show how an alien insect can engineer host tissues in ways that increase plantation invasibility. If unsupported, the same tests will delimit when plant-mediated interactions amongst alien herbivores are neutral or antagonistic rather than facilitative. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Assessing the accuracy and stability of variable importance in species distribution modelling algorithms through sample perturbations
items.abstract: Variable importance derived from species distribution modelling (SDM) is widely used to identify key environmental drivers of species distributions. However, the reliability of these inferences has rarely been systematically evaluated, particularly with respect to their sensitivity to individual occurrences. Here, we used virtual species and developed a sample perturbations diagnostic framework, in which each occurrence was systematically removed (leave‐one‐out) to assess how small changes in the input data affect variable importance inference. Using this framework, we evaluated and compared ten SDM algorithms across multiple scenarios. We constructed a set of evaluation metrics to quantify both the accuracy of driver identification and the stability of permutation importance estimates, defined as their variability under sample perturbations. We further investigated the sample level mechanisms underlying instability. Our results showed that random forest (RF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), and maximum entropy (Maxent) achieved the best overall performance. RF exhibited the relatively high inferential accuracy and stability, but showed limited ability to differentiate the relative importance of environmental variables. GBM and Maxent achieved slightly lower accuracy than RF, but were more stable and effective for distinguishing the relative contributions of different variables. Instead, several algorithms displayed relatively high accuracy but were sensitive to sample perturbations. Scenario analyses indicated that stability generally increased under conditions of high sample sizes, low geographical sampling bias, and moderate prevalence. Highly influential occurrences were not necessarily associated with extreme environmental conditions. Removal experiments further demonstrated that variable importance inference in several algorithms was sensitive to a relatively small subset of occurrences, highlighting the disproportionate contribution of these occurrences. Overall, this study provides a sample level diagnostic framework for evaluating the reliability of variable importance in SDM, offering practical guidance for improving the interpretability of environmental driver inference in ecological research and conservation applications.

items.title: Hunters in Danger: Evolutionary Diversity and Conservation Priorities in Carnivore Species of the American Continent
items.abstract: Aim Many mammals of the order Carnivora are key ecosystem predators. In the American continent, they have a complex biogeographical history, shaped by processes of colonization and adaptive radiation that have generated a high diversity of lineages. However, under the global biodiversity crisis, this group faces increasing extinction risk, and conservation efforts have focused mainly on species richness while neglecting evolutionary relationships. We aimed to assess the distribution of evolutionary diversity in carnivores of the American continent and its relationship with biological and geographical variables to recognize species and areas with unique evolutionary value. Location American continent. Methods We evaluated 104 carnivore species of the Americas. Using data from public literature, we calculated Evolutionary Distinctiveness (ED), Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (EDGE; EDGE2), and Biogeographically weighted Evolutionary Distinctiveness (BED) metrics. In addition, we explored the relationship between evolutionary scores with body size, altitudinal and latitudinal distribution of species, and mapped spatial patterns of richness and evolutionary metrics to identify priority areas for conservation. Results The evolutionary diversity of carnivores was unevenly distributed across regions and taxonomic groups. In terrestrial species, all evolutionary scores decreased with altitude, and only ED followed a unimodal pattern with latitude, concentrating in the tropical belt; in marine species, ED clustered in the temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere. A positive relationship was detected between body size and ED in marine species, and a negative relationship was observed with BED in terrestrial species and across all carnivores. Spatial patterns of richness were consistent with those of ED, EDGE and EDGE2 scores, but differed from those obtained with BED scores. Main Conclusion Our findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating evolutionary metrics into the prioritization of American carnivores as a means to safeguard their evolutionary history and to optimize conservation planning and resource allocation from a comprehensive perspective.

items.title: Metabolic ecology and habitat stability explain the disproportionately high species richness in standing waters
items.abstract: The metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) conceptualizes that temperature is the primary driver of species richness, a pattern well supported in terrestrial taxa but less certain for freshwater organisms. Limited global‐scale evidence and frequent violations of MTE's assumptions, particularly regarding the stationarity of body size and abundance, further undermine its applicability. In freshwater systems, body size and abundance are tightly linked to dispersal and range size, which differ markedly between running‐water (lotic) and standing‐water (lentic) species, as proposed by the Habitat‐Stability–Dispersal Hypothesis (HSDH). Adaptations to habitat stability may therefore generate distinct biogeographical patterns of traits and modify richness–temperature relationships predicted by MTE. Utilizing comprehensive global functional, phylogenetic, and distributional data on dragonfly and damselfly species (83%) and habitat information (46%), we tested MTE predictions for lentic versus lotic species. Lotic species richness followed MTE expectations (slope: −0.469) more closely than lentic species richness (slope: −0.283). The proportion of lentic species in an assemblage was the strongest predictor of deviation in the species richness–temperature relationship ( R 2 = 38%). Assemblages dominated by lentic species clustered in climatically unstable regions and mainly included smaller‐bodied species with larger ranges. Phylogenetic comparative analysis shows a strong phylogenetic signal in habitat preference, with the most species‐rich and northerly distributed families comprising predominantly lentic species. Our findings suggest that adaptations to habitat stability facilitated the colonization and persistence of lentic species in harsh and fluctuating climates, both past and present, resulting in largely divergent species richness patterns of lentic and lotic odonates. Integrating HSDH‐related traits (body and range size) not only substantially improves the explanatory power of the MTE but also reveals a trait syndrome with broad implications for the biogeography and climate change responses of freshwater communities.

items.title: From patterns to predictions: a framework for the spatial epidemiology of wildlife diseases
items.abstract: Wildlife diseases pose a significant threat to biodiversity conservation, public health, and livestock. Spatial epidemiology provides a robust framework to understand disease dynamics and guide policy and management. However, the rapid proliferation of spatial methods has largely occurred in isolation across disciplines, leaving the field without a unified framework that connects these approaches and clarifies their strengths, limitations, and applications. The spatial epidemiology workflow includes three main steps: 1) descriptive analysis of spatial patterns; 2) exploration of observed patterns through explicative analyses; and 3) prediction of pathogen distribution and spread. Descriptive analysis, such as disease mapping and clustering analysis, identifies spatial patterns and informs hypotheses about potential risk factors. Subsequently, explicative analyses can link pathogen presence to ecological or anthropogenic drivers and explain spatiotemporal dynamics. Drivers of pathogen transmission can be further understood through mechanistic models, ranging from population‐level Susceptible‐Infected‐Removed (SIR) frameworks to individual‐ or group‐based SIR approaches such as metapopulation and network models that can incorporate host behavior and social structure. Molecular epidemiology, through genetic variant identification and phylogenetic mapping, can identify outbreak origins and host linkages. Lastly, predictions of pathogen distribution and spread are enabled by ecological niche models and species distribution models, which project potential pathogen distributions based on ecological, geographical, and/or anthropogenic factors, and by mechanistic simulations that parameterize pathogen spread processes to predict expansion over space and time. System‐based simulations focus on population‐level dynamics, while agent‐based simulations incorporate individual‐level dynamics, offering detailed insights into pathogen spread and control measures. Consequently, the integration of descriptive analyses, explicative procedures, and predictive models provides a robust framework for addressing the challenges posed by wildlife diseases and developing management and control measures.

items.title: Human pressure, habitat heterogeneity and species traits jointly determine the level of dark diversity in coastal fish communities
items.abstract: Understanding how anthropogenic pressures and environmental gradients shape coastal fish communities is a central question in biogeography and marine conservation. Yet, the set of species expected to occur at a site given ecological conditions but being absent – the so‐called dark diversity – has received far less attention than observed species, even if they hold key information about local extirpations and conservation effectiveness. Quantifying dark diversity in the sea is particularly challenging because many species are rare, cryptobenthic or mobile, while sampling effort is rarely standardized. Here we combined 930 environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected at 401 sites along 2000 km of the French Mediterranean coast with fine‐scale mapping of habitats, anthropogenic pressures and protection levels. Using a Bayesian model of dark diversity affinity (DDA) that explicitly controls for sampling effort, we decomposed the correlates of species absences into site characteristics and species traits, separating dispersal‐related from sensitivity‐related signals. At the site level, fishing effort, marine traffic, and artificial habitats were associated with greater DDA, so a deficit of species, whereas protected areas and diverse natural habitats were associated with lower DDA, increasing the likelihood of observing more complete fish communities. At the species level, demersal and predator species, together with those bearing their eggs (e.g. many elasmobranchs) compared to species with demersal or pelagic eggs, exhibited the highest DDA, suggesting local extirpations linked to a combination of limited dispersal and higher sensitivity to cumulative pressures. Beyond the creation of marine protected areas, preserving habitat heterogeneity and mitigating coastal pressures therefore emerge as essential levers to limit the local erosion of fish biodiversity. More broadly, coupling eDNA with a sampling‐effort‐corrected DDA framework offers a transferable benchmark to evaluate where, and for which species, conservation efforts are most needed.

items.title: ZonationR: An R interface to the Zonation software for reproducible spatial conservation prioritisation workflows
items.abstract: Systematic conservation planning provides a science‐based framework for defining conservation goals and supporting transparent spatial decision‐making under limited resources. Within this framework, spatial conservation prioritisation tools are widely used to identify areas of high biodiversity value by integrating information on species distributions, connectivity, costs, and other factors into spatially explicit recommendations. ‘Zonation' is one of the leading software tools in this field, producing hierarchical priority rankings of landscapes based on conservation value. However, its standard workflow typically relies on manual steps for data preparation, execution, and post‐processing, which can become inefficient and difficult to reproduce when multiple scenarios are analysed, limiting accessibility and broader uptake. We introduce ‘ZonationR', an R package that provides a streamlined interface to the ‘Zonation' software, enabling fully reproducible and automated spatial prioritisation workflows. The package integrates the entire analysis pipeline, encompassing input preparation, execution of ‘Zonation', and post‐processing, while supporting both single‐variant and multi‐variant workflows. ‘ZonationR' also provides tools to explore and interpret outputs, including priority maps, feature performance curves, cost summaries, feature representation metrics, and similarity assessments between prioritisation solutions. By linking directly to the original ‘Zonation' engine, the package enables users to benefit from ongoing methodological developments in ‘Zonation' and access its functionality through a transparent, script‐based workflow, thereby reducing technical barriers to running and understanding spatial prioritisation analyses. Beyond these advantages, its integration within the R environment supports iterative testing of conservation scenarios and more rigorous assessment of methodological decisions, while facilitating seamless connections with wider ecological workflows (e.g. species distribution modelling). As conservation planning increasingly relies on large, complex, multi‐source datasets and integrative approaches, such integration is essential for enabling robust, transparent, and reproducible decision‐making across spatial scales.

items.title: Predicting Red List categories reveals hidden extinction risk in one of the world’s most diverse freshwater invertebrate families
items.abstract: Global Red List assessments suggest that approximately 25% of freshwater animal species are at risk of extinction. However, these estimates remain tentative due to insufficient assessments of numerous species-rich invertebrate groups in neglected ecosystems, such as springs and subterranean waters. Including these overlooked taxa in extinction risk assessments is crucial for conservation. To address this gap, we predicted extinction risk in Hydrobiidae, the most diverse family of freshwater gastropods. We compiled occurrence, environmental, and trait data for 876 hydrobiid species and employed deep-learning models trained on International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List assessments to predict extinction risk for 403 Data Deficient and Not Evaluated species. We further analyzed the relative importance and effect of geographic, environmental, and biological predictors and compared extinction risk across habitats, ecoregions, and subfamily clades. Predictive models indicated that extinction risk within Hydrobiidae is underestimated; incorporating predicted assessments suggests that over 60% of species may be threatened. Geographic range attributes, particularly area of occupancy, were the strongest predictors of extinction risk, followed by climate and habitat. Threatened species are concentrated in springs and lakes, and in several freshwater ecoregions of the Mediterranean Basin, North Africa, and western North America. Hydrobiidae exceed most plant and vertebrate groups in both the proportion of endangered evolutionary history and the number of Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (EDGE) species. Our findings demonstrate that predictive assessments can substantially expand Red List coverage and reveal overlooked patterns of extinction risk across understudied taxa, particularly freshwater invertebrates.
