items.title: Scale‐dependent assembly shapes taxon‐dependent responses of soil microbes to island isolation and area
items.abstract: The theory of island biogeography (TIB) remains contentious for microbes, as their immense dispersal potential and microscopic size may decouple diversity from classic isolation/area effects. We explicitly tested TIB scaling rules for soil bacteria and fungi across 20 oceanic islands using a rigorous multi‐scale framework that integrated high‐resolution ASV analysis, coverage‐based diversity estimation, and phylogenetic null models. We found that geographic isolation emerged as the predominant driver of microbial diversity, yielding consistent negative species–solation relationships (SIRs, where species richness decreases with isolation) across scales and most taxonomic groups, reflecting pervasive dispersal limitation. In contrast, species–area relationships (SARs, where species richness increases with area) at the island scale were largely attributable to sampling intensity. After standardizing sampling effort and integrating local‐scale (mean plot ASV richness) analyses, significant positive SARs disappeared for all groups except arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. This pattern reflects the unique ecological dependence of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi on host‐mediated environmental heterogeneity. Community assembly analyses using iCAMP and variation partitioning consistently revealed that while dispersal limitation dominated community assembly (62.1–81.5% of the variation), homogeneous selection intensified on more isolated islands for most microbes. As island area increased, environmental filtering was relaxed, yet spatial assembly processes diverged: dispersal limitation intensified for most fungi, whereas homogeneous selection became more prominent for most bacteria. These results demonstrate that geographic isolation drives microbial diversity, yet its effects are scale‐dependent and taxon‐specific. These findings highlight the need to incorporate scale‐ and lineage‐specific assembly processes into TIB for microbial community.

items.title: Agricultural transformation threatens thermal refuges: risk assessment for lacertid lizards in Mediterranean olive groves
items.abstract: Agricultural intensification and the abandonment of traditional management practices in Mediterranean olive groves have replaced old-growth trees and traditional structures, such as dry-stone walls, across thousands of hectares with high-density plantations. This transformation of traditional landscapes threatens biodiversity by reducing critical refuges for fauna, including reptiles, which rely on these microhabitats for thermoregulation. This study investigates the thermal properties of two key refuges in traditional olive groves in southern Spain: hollow trunks of old olive trees and dry-stone walls. Temperatures were recorded every 10 min over a three-month summer period and compared with shaded air temperatures to evaluate their capacity to buffer extreme heat. Field temperatures were compared with published selected thermal ranges (Tsel) and critical thermal maximum (CTmax) for three Mediterranean lizards, Psammodromus algirus , Podarcis hispanicus , and Acanthodactylus erythrurus . Daily temperature range was greater in shaded air than in either refuge type, whereas differences between walls and trunks were not significant, indicating that both structures buffered thermal fluctuations. No temperatures inside hollow trunks exceeded published CTmax estimates for any species during the study period. In contrast, wall temperatures exceeded CTmax estimates for all three species at some point during the study. These findings highlight the importance of traditional olive groves as systems that maintain diverse thermal refuges with complementary properties. Their loss may reduce microclimatic heterogeneity and limit the range of thermal conditions available to reptiles. Conservation strategies should prioritize retaining old trees and restoring dry-stone walls to maintain diverse thermal refuges in Mediterranean agricultural landscapes under climate change. items.title: Declines in dryland woody vegetation following an extended dry decade
items.abstract: Changes in temperature, rainfall regimes and water availability, as part of global climate change, lead to increased drought stress, especially in dry ecosystems. Yet empirical evidence of how woody vegetation responds to such climate drying remains scarce. We examined changes in woody cover and species composition across 71 woodland and shrubland sites, spanning the east Mediterranean climatic gradient, resurveyed a decade apart (2008–2009 and 2018–2019). The studied decade was characterized by reduced rainfall and a shorter rainy season combined with consistent warming, resulting in increasing aridity. Woody cover declined in 52% of sites and increased in 24% of them. The magnitude of decline was greatest in arid regions and was strongly predicted by mean annual precipitation. Model selection identified species richness as a stabilizing factor: sites with high species richness experienced smaller losses or maintained stable woody cover. At the species level, we identified seven dominant tree, shrub and sub‐shrub species. Of these, Quercus coccifera var. calliprinos showed consistent increases in cover, correlated with the rainfall gradient, whereas the cover of Pistacia lentiscus , Calicotome villosa , Cistus spp., and Sarcopoterium spinosum declined. The cover of Phillyrea latifolia and Rhamnus spp. was relatively stable. However, climatic variability explained only a small portion of the change in cover of each of the dominant species. Synthesis . Our results reveal a shift from the well‐documented trajectory of secondary woodland regeneration towards regional declines in woody cover under intensifying aridity. Our findings provide rare field‐based evidence that species richness enhances vegetation resistance to climate drying.

items.title: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
items.abstract: Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co-occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep-sea corals (Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila, and Madracis interjecta) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090-2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long-term conservation action to protect these important habitats.

items.title: An Open Occurrence Dataset for European Subterranean Spiders
items.abstract: Motivation Spiders are common inhabitants of caves and other subterranean habitats, where they play key ecological roles as generalist predators and strongly influence local food webs. They have been instrumental as model organisms for testing various eco‐evolutionary hypotheses. Furthermore, strictly subterranean species exhibiting narrow ranges and high endemism are particularly significant for conservation planning and vulnerability assessments. Although high‐quality data are essential for research on and conservation of subterranean spiders, such information remains scarce, especially regarding distribution patterns. To help fill this gap, we screened the literature, unpublished records and open datasets to compile georeferenced occurrences of subterranean spiders across caves and other subterranean habitats throughout Europe. To illustrate one potential application of the compiled dataset, we also present a prediction of subterranean spider richness patterns across Europe using stacked species distribution models. Main Types of Variables Contained The European Subterranean Spider Dataset (ESSD) comprises 31,498 records of 637 subterranean‐dwelling spider species, covering a range of information including taxonomy, locality details (such as location name, country, geographic coordinates, type of subterranean habitat) and reference information for each record. All variables are coded using the Darwin Core Standard, ensuring interoperability with the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and other biodiversity databases. Spatial Location and Grain The collected data are distributed across 42 countries within the European continent, with varying spatial uncertainty. Most coordinates of localities are taken at the cave entrance (uncertainty of ca. 10 m), or at the nearest hamlet when precise coordinates are not available (uncertainty of ca. 1 km). Time Period and Grain The data represent information made available between 1881 and 2026. Major Taxa and Level of Measurement 637 species (including morphospecies under description) of subterranean spiders across 28 families. These species span a gradient of ecological dependence on subterranean habitats, ranging from species still able to exploit surface habitats to obligate subterranean dwellers. Software Format The dataset is available in .csv format in Figshare data repository (available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30696173 ) and in GBIF ( https://doi.org/10.15468/f4xjdb ).

items.title: Multi-scale modeling of continent-wide tracking data confirms the importance of landscape mosaics for the European wildcat
items.abstract: Context Land use change is a major threat to the persistence of wildlife in human-dominated landscapes, making the knowledge of the amount and spatial configuration of suitable habitat essential for conservation. The European wildcat ( Felis silvestris ) currently persists in fragmented populations and faces ever increasing human pressure. Objectives We modeled and mapped suitable wildcat habitats at the continental scale, to identify opportunities and constraints for its conservation. Methods We compiled a large telemetry dataset comprising 200 wildcats across Europe and developed multi-scale habitat suitability models using Maxent. Habitat selection was analyzed at two hierarchical levels: home-range placement within the wider landscape and selection within the established home ranges. Results At both levels, wildcats selected broadleaved forests, mixed forests, and grasslands, while avoiding landscapes dominated by large continuous forests. For home-range placement, they preferred lower terrain ruggedness and less intensive agriculture. Within the home ranges, wildcats selected forest edges and small woody features. Conclusions Our results highlight the importance of heterogeneous forest–grassland mosaics habitats. More than half of the predicted suitable habitat occurred outside protected areas, highlighting the need for effective conservation strategies beyond their borders. Predictions of suitable areas should, however, be interpreted cautiously in regions where environmental conditions extend beyond those represented in the calibration data. By providing the first continental-scale habitat suitability map based on a large European telemetry dataset, our study offers a spatial foundation for identifying conservation priorities and supporting the long-term connectivity and recovery of wildcat populations.

items.title: Contrasting climatic niche structure and projected suitability for Canada lynx and bobcat
items.abstract: We asked whether the Canada lynx ( Lynx canadensis ) and the bobcat ( Lynx rufus ) differ in the internal structure of their occupied climatic niches and whether any difference translates into contrasting mid-century projections across North America. We calibrated ensemble species distribution models on 6,721 Canada lynx and 9,030 bobcat records with six climatic predictors per species, compared them in environmental space, and projected suitability to 2041–2060 under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways and three global climate models. The two species occupy divergent observed climatic niches, and the difference is not explained by the climates available to each. The models are dominated by different climatic axes rather than by different positions along a shared one: isothermality for the Canada lynx and cold-quarter potential evapotranspiration for the bobcat. They also differ in breadth, with three biomes holding almost all Canada lynx records, compared with seven for the bobcat. Both occupied niches extend to the edge of the climate available in North America, indicating that the broader climatic tolerance of either species may not be fully resolved from this continent alone. Projections diverge: suitable climate for the Canada lynx contracts, with losses concentrated in the alpine and subalpine homologs of its lowland core. Under the design we report, bobcat suitability expands into boreal biomes it currently barely occupies, and the area suitable for both more than doubles. Because projections depend on where background data are drawn, we repeated the workflow under four pseudo-absence schemes: the direction of change held for the Canada lynx but reversed for the bobcat, and we report both.

items.title: A Multidimensional Climatic Variability Hypothesis for Terrestrial Ectotherms
items.abstract: Aim The climatic variability hypothesis (CVH) predicts that ectotherms exposed to greater climatic variability evolve broader physiological tolerances, but its application to biogeography has been dominated by thermal traits. Here, the author argue that the CVH empirical testing warrants expansion beyond the thermal axis, using an existing mechanistic niche framework. Location Global. Major Taxa Studied Terrestrial ectotherms. Main Conclusions Evidence for thermal tolerance breadth is extensive and generally supports CVH predictions, but exceptions exist, largely driven by taxon‐specific responses and climatic extremes rather than variability. Evidence for hydric and energetic traits remains more limited but shows that water balance and metabolic traits vary across geographic gradients. These axes interact mechanistically, that is, dehydration can reduce thermal tolerance and performance, while water limitation can restrict the activity and foraging needed to meet metabolic costs. Testing these interactions at the distributional level requires models that capture them, yet current correlative species distribution models do not incorporate these interacting constraints. Mechanistic and hybrid models provide a way for integrating physiological data into forecasts of range limits and vulnerability to climate change. The major empirical gap is the scarcity of datasets that measure thermal, hydric and energetic traits simultaneously in the same groups of organisms across environmental gradients. A multidimensional CVH provides a testable framework for improving mechanistic understanding and prediction of terrestrial ectotherm responses to global change.

items.title: Embracing ignorance: tackling biodiversity knowledge shortfalls
items.abstract: Global biodiversity information suffers from gaps, biases, and uncertainty over time and space, afflicting all taxonomic groups. Incomplete or biased data introduce uncertainty into models of biodiversity trends, potentially generating faulty inferences with knock-on effects for conservation. We revisit how the limitations of biodiversity knowledge are conceptualised, expanding the current classification to encompass eleven major shortfalls spanning taxonomic, ecological, evolutionary, and biocultural aspects, and examine the impediments that limit progress in reducing them. Information gaps have been moulded by our capacity and willingness to collect data, which are constrained by a series of financial, taxonomic, and technological impediments that vary across regions and taxa. Addressing these challenges is crucial for understanding biodiversity patterns and processes and developing effective conservation actions.

items.title: Two decades of Landsat images reveal spatial and temporal dynamics of invasion and improve species distribution models
items.abstract: Developing accurate and cost‐effective methods to detect and predict the spread of invasive species remains an ongoing challenge. Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used to predict invasion under current and future climates and inform management strategies. However, occurrence datasets are often spatially and temporally biased due to unstructured and opportunistic data collection. Remote sensing of individual species over broad spatial and temporal scales has become increasingly feasible with the accumulation of satellite images and the development of convolutional neural networks. In this study, we used 21 years of archival Landsat satellite imagery (2000–2020) to train a land use/land cover (LULC) classification algorithm using a temporal convolutional neural network to predict occurrence of the invasive species, leafy spurge ( Euphorbia virgata ), across Minnesota. We validated our predictions with an independent dataset. First, we show that leafy spurge has expanded from 1067 km 2 in 2000–2002 to 7156 km 2 in 2018–2020, a 570% increase. Drought severity modulated the predicted area invaded and was associated with fluctuations over time. Second, we tracked changes in probability over time for individual pixels and showed that invasion has been concentrated in two largely disjunct regions that differ in climate. Third, our remotely sensed predicted occurrence dataset and community science dataset were closer to roadsides, suggesting that roadside disturbance facilitates invasion. Last, we showed that SDMs built using remotely sensed occurrences had higher discrimination, were less overfit, and performed better outside of urban areas. Overall, 21 years of archival satellite imagery showed rapid expansion in two geographically distinct regions, invasion associated with roads, and improved predictions of invasion.

items.title: Revealing the Widespread Bias of Extinction Risk in the Antarctic and the Southern Ocean
items.abstract: Accelerating environmental change in the Antarctic and Southern Ocean (ASO) necessitates robust extinction risk assessments to inform conservation priorities. Nevertheless, no systematic, region-wide baseline of extinction risk currently exists for tracking ASO biodiversity responses to ongoing change, a significant barrier to global biodiversity monitoring. Here, we conducted the first ASO-wide synthesis of current extinction risk knowledge for plants, animals and Fungi. This included examining biases in current assessments, the distribution of Threatened species and their associated threats. Using a data-inclusive workflow, we compiled 8908 assessments representing 4970 species, more than doubling the number of ASO species assessed compared with any single source. As expected, assessments were heavily biased towards vertebrates (58% assessed), while invertebrates, despite their ecological prevalence, were markedly underrepresented (6% assessed). Among vertebrates, mammals had the highest proportion of Threatened species (26%). Birds within the ASO were disproportionately Threatened (25%) compared to the global average (11%), with the greatest threat for ASO species being 'Biological Resource Use'. The sub-Antarctic Islands had the highest density of both Threatened species and assessment effort, whereas many Antarctic species remain unassessed. Additionally, Threatened species have the lowest protected area coverage of any conservation status. These pronounced assessment biases highlight the need for more balanced, representative and data-inclusive extinction risk assessments to be able to effectively detect conservation status change. This work represents an important step in ensuring ASO representation in global biodiversity monitoring frameworks, strengthening the capacity of these frameworks to detect, attribute and respond to future biodiversity changes.

items.title: Importance of scale in seascape habitat suitability modeling: Predicting species distributions in changing ecosystems
items.abstract: Habitat suitability models (HSMs) use landscape metrics to describe patterns in species distributions, quantify the success of habitat restoration, and model species responses to change. Within a particular level of organization, the spatial scale of effect at which habitat is integrated and incorporated into HSMs can influence model performance. However, scale optimization can be time consuming and requires high-quality data across spatial scales. As such, it is not widely applied in suitability models and is particularly rare in marine studies. In coastal and marine landscapes, or seascapes, rapidly changing seascape metrics and environmental contexts can disrupt known species-seascape relationships and complicate evaluations of habitat quality. Studying the effect of scale on species suitability models in these systems allows for greater predictive power and better understanding of the multiscale processes that drive species distributions. We use quantitative species abundance from a Louisiana Gulf coast estuary along with both drone and satellite-derived habitat data to model species-habitat relationships across a range of measurement scales. Using this approach, we identify optimal measurement scales for population-level HSMs for Penaeus setiferus (white shrimp) and Callinectes sapidus (blue crabs) and identify key species-habitat relationships. Within the range of scales considered (20-600-m radius), blue crab HSMs had the highest predictive power at 150 m. White shrimp showed high predictive power at both 120 m and 300 m in drone and satellite-based analyses, respectively. Our models show that white shrimp have a positive association with Avicennia germinans (black mangroves), a range-expanding foundation species rapidly encroaching onto the Spartina alterniflora marshes in Louisiana. This approach generates predictive HSMs for two key fisheries species on the Louisiana coast and helps define their relationship to ongoing changes in their habitat. Future seascape suitability studies should test across spatial scales to optimize the predictive power of their models.

items.title: Plant invasions in Natura 2000 habitats in Poland are driven primarily by macroclimatic factors
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 65-85 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.187603 Authors: Szymon Święcicki, Natalia Chojnowska, Łukasz Kozub, Iwona Dembicz Abstract: Invasive plants pose an ecological threat around the world. Their influence can also be observed in protected areas such as the European Ecological Network Natura 2000. Although invasions can endanger protected habitats, the specific impact of invasive species in such areas and the factors that determine their spread remain understudied. This study aimed to analyse the factors influencing the probability of plant invasion in five groups of habitat types protected under the EU Habitats Directive, based on Polish State Monitoring of Natura 2000 data. A total of 2,096 monitoring sites, with a balanced distribution across the country, were analysed, belonging to broadleaf forests, riverine habitats, dry grasslands, mesic and wet grasslands, and mires. The study confirmed the presence of 45 invasive species and two potentially invasive species. The most frequently observed species were Impatiens parviflora, Prunus serotina, Solidago gigantea, Erigeron canadensis, Solidago canadensis, and Bidens frondosa. The correlation between the presence of invasive species in monitored Natura 2000 sites and 38 variables was then analysed. The probability of invasion was much higher in regions with milder and wetter winters and, at the same time, in areas with a more continental climate. The importance of large rivers and their valleys and major roads as corridors facilitating plant invasions was also confirmed. Moreover, this study demonstrated the effectiveness of the State Monitoring Programme in detecting invasive species and analysing invasions. The programme could be used to inform the planning of future invasion management and prevention strategies. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Measuring the edges of species' geographic ranges
items.abstract: The fundamental unit of spatial ecology is a species range: the geographical area that it occupies. Species ranges are delineated by range edges (also known as boundaries or limits). Why range edges occur where they do and not elsewhere, and what makes them move, has been an active area of research since the 19th century. In the present day, range edge dynamics are an important metric of biodiversity's response to climate change, as species shift toward the poles to track their climatic niches. Yet there are many methods for measuring range edges and quantifying their displacement. Here I describe common methods for describing range edge positions and apply them to example data for a bird species and a fish species, using some of the most popular datasets in climate biogeography: the Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count and a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration bottom trawl survey. I show that the choice of range edge metric influences where range edge positions are estimated to occur; whether they are estimated to be shifting over time; and the estimated rate of shift. The lack of standardized metrics for range edges has likely shaped statistics reported in synthesis studies that measured overall biodiversity responses to climate change and global rates of range shifts. Through simulation, I found that reliably detecting range edge shifts may require decades of data or more, suggesting that many global change studies in this field are underpowered. Pairing metrics to research questions, sharing raw data and code, and conducting power analyses before reporting statistically significant results will all help to minimize this issue. Going forward, the field of biogeography should confront the degree to which ad hoc methods have influenced our understanding of range edge dynamics and move towards standardized metrics.

items.title: DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California's insect biodiversity remains undiscovered
items.abstract: Insects are the most diverse terrestrial organisms, yet they are underrepresented in large‐scale conservation assessments. To address this gap, the California Insect Barcoding Initiative is developing a publicly accessible, statewide DNA‐barcode reference library for California insects to support scalable surveys, establish baseline biodiversity measurements, and generate potential distribution maps that inform conservation planning. Specimens are collected with a hybrid strategy that combines standardized Malaise trapping, to enable replicable sampling, and opportunistic collecting, to maximize taxonomic coverage. Using samples collected primarily from 2022–2024 at 72 longer‐term Malaise trap sites, coupled with collecting using varied methods at 454 additional locations across California, we have barcoded over one million specimens. Preliminary completeness analyses suggest that current sampling captures roughly 65–69% of the fauna, implying a conservative minimum of circa 61 000 insect species in California, as delimited by their DNA barcode sequence. Using all sequenced specimen records, we generated rule‐based spatial range interpolations constrained by ecoregion and vegetation type, and used these to infer spatial patterns in insect species richness across the state. We identify areas of both high and low potential species richness, with current peaks in the Southern California Mountains ecoregion and the Mojave Basin and Range ecoregion. Our species richness estimates and spatial patterns are explicitly provisional and are expected to evolve as sampling gaps are addressed. Finally, we make all sequence data, specimen images, and occurrence records publicly available via the Barcode of Life Datasystem. This ongoing effort constitutes the first large‐scale DNA barcode‐based survey for California insects, providing an expandable foundation for tracking temporal change, testing drivers of insect diversity, and prioritizing regions for conservation and targeted inventory.

items.title: Behavioural Plasticity Is Associated With Climate Tracking in Birds
items.abstract: Aim To test whether behavioural plasticity is associated with birds' ability to track climate change and whether this relationship differs among spatial gradients and range positions. Location Global. Time Period Range‐shift and feeding‐related behavioural plasticity observations compiled from 1890 to 2018. Major Taxa Studied Birds. Methods We combined 5733 population‐level range‐shift observations from 1096 bird species in the BioShifts database with a global dataset of avian feeding innovations, a proxy for behavioural plasticity. Using Bayesian phylogenetic mixed‐effects models fitted separately for latitudinal and elevational gradients and for range centroids, leading edges and trailing edges, we tested whether innovation modified the coupling between range‐shift and local climate change velocity, while controlling for key life‐history traits, environmental covariates and phylogenetic non‐independence. Results At latitudinal range centroids, innovative species showed tighter coupling between range‐shift and climate velocities than non‐innovative species, but this association was not supported at leading or trailing edges. Innovativeness was not associated with elevational tracking at centroids or leading edges but was positively associated with tracking at trailing edges. Tracking probability declined as climate velocity increased along both gradients, but innovativeness buffered this decline at latitudinal range centroids and elevational trailing edge. Other life‐history and environmental covariates showed limited associations with climate tracking. Main Conclusions Feeding‐related behavioural plasticity is associated with stronger climate tracking in birds at latitudinal range centroids and elevational trailing edges. These associations vary across spatial gradients and range positions, suggesting that the contribution of behavioural plasticity to redistribution depends on the ecological processes governing different parts of species' ranges. Incorporating behavioural traits alongside environmental constraints and range position into climate‐change vulnerability assessments could improve predictions of species redistribution under warming.

items.title: Mapping diversity through geographical, environmental and attribute spaces
items.abstract: Understanding biodiversity patterns requires integrating information across the interrelated dimensions that organize life. Species occupy specific regions in geographic space, respond to environmental conditions and vary within attribute (or trait) spaces that are shaped by their ecological and evolutionary histories. However, most analyses address these dimensions independently, limiting our ability to understand how constraints in one space interrelate to patterns in another. Developing approaches that explicitly quantify and connect the geometry of these spaces should unify the study of biodiversity across scales and dimensions. We implement such a framework in the letsR R package by constructing a triad of presence–absence matrices (PAMs) representing geographic, environmental and attribute spaces. A concise set of functions computes geometry‐aware descriptors such as centrality, frequency, isolation and border proximity, and allows these descriptors to be propagated among spaces through explicit connectors. This design builds on the letsR architecture and integrates with functions to facilitate macroecological analysis. Using global terrestrial mammals as a model group, we illustrate how descriptors derived from environmental space can be mapped back into geographic and attribute spaces. This approach reveals where particular regions of climatic space are common or rare, how isolated they are and how these properties influence species richness across dimensions. This novel implementation lowers the barrier to reproducible, geometry‐aware analyses and enables direct tests of how constraints in one space influence diversity in others, advancing a more integrated understanding of macroecological and macroevolutionary patterns.

items.title: Decoupling environmental suitability from realized recruitment through ontogenetic environmental filtering in a long‐lived Mediterranean palm species
items.abstract: Long‐lived plants facing anthropogenic disturbance often exhibit recruitment failure despite persistent reproductive adults, generating extinction debt masked by longevity. However, whether adult presence reliably reflects environmental suitability for recruitment remains unclear. Here, we examine ontogenetic niche differentiation and its consequences for recruitment in Jubaea chilensis , an endangered long‐lived Mediterranean palm with an aging population. We assigned individuals within the largest known population to four ontogenetic stages and characterized their environmental niches using climatic, edaphic, topographic and vegetation variables. We then applied spatial and multivariate analyses, including random forest models to evaluate environmental segregation and identify predictors of seedling establishment. Age classes occupied significantly different environmental niches, with the greatest differentiation between seedlings and reproductive adults. Saplings and adult differentiation reflected mainly topographic variables at landscape scale, whereas seedling establishment was primarily predicted by microhabitat conditions (vegetation cover heterogeneity, east‐facing slope orientation and soil texture). This pattern is consistent with niche reconfiguring throughout the life cycle, suggesting that adult occurrence and recruitment suitability respond to distinct environmental conditions. This divergence may be further intensified by ongoing climate change, particularly Mediterranean aridification, progressively narrowing the environmental space available for successful recruitment. Over one‐fifth of sampled individuals occupied high‐suitability sites without recruitment, suggesting that ontogenetic niche shifts are associated with a spatial decoupling between adult persistence and recruitment, consistent with demographic collapse independent of habitat degradation. This failure is likely mediated by insufficient effective seed dispersal, as the sole disperser Octodon degus preys on most seeds before dispersal. Conservation strategies based solely on adult distribution may therefore overestimate effective habitat and underestimate extinction risk in long‐lived species.

items.title: Intensification and Spatial Reorganization of Drought Risks for Global Rainfed Crops Under Climate Change
items.abstract: Rainfed agriculture covers roughly 80% of global cropland and supplies more than half of global food production, yet uncertainty in how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone water deficits and crop losses impedes robust risk assessment. Here, we establish an integrated, production‐weighted assessment framework coupling SPEI, SSI, and 12 GGCMI3 crop models to trace how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone deficits and crop losses, explicitly separating affected area, conditional yield loss, and accumulated production loss across rainfed maize, soybean, and wheat. By 2070–2099, opposing‐direction SPEI–SSI change classes occupied 6.8%–28.4% of rainfed area across crops under SSP1‐2.6/default CO 2 and 26.6%–48.2% under SSP5‐8.5/default CO 2 . Comparison with fixed‐2015 CO 2 experiments (7.5%–27.6% and 21.7%–34.9%, respectively) indicates that elevated CO 2 substantially expanded the spatial footprint of this hydrometeorological decoupling. Historically, SSI‐defined drought affected 12–16 million ha year −1 and was associated with annual production losses of 5–12 Mt year −1 (1.6–2.0% year −1 ). Under default CO 2 , affected area increased to 14–21 million ha under SSP1‐2.6 and 19–27 million ha under SSP5‐8.5, with production losses of 6–12 and 9–12 Mt year −1 , respectively. Under SSP5‐8.5, median loss rates were higher under fixed‐2015 than default CO 2 for maize (3.33 vs. 1.96% year −1 ), soybean (4.22 vs. 2.84% year −1 ) and wheat (5.41 vs. 2.90% year −1 ), as elevated CO 2 reduces stomatal water loss and thus mitigates drought impacts, whereas SSP1‐2.6 estimates were similar. Severe drought became the largest loss contributor under both pathways and CO 2 settings. Under default CO 2 , loss increases clustered in Central America, northeastern Brazil, western Europe and southern Africa; fixed‐2015 CO 2 broadened the area of robust grid‐cell loss increases. These results show that drought‐related production losses are spatially uneven and sensitive to the modeled CO 2 response, highlighting the value of crop‐ and region‐specific risk assessment.

items.title: A systematic review of avian influenza virus transmission models: Gaps and opportunities
items.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) increasingly threatens wild birds, poultry, non‐human mammals and humans, yet gaps and opportunities in avian influenza virus (AIV) transmission modelling have not been comprehensively synthesized. We reviewed 182 articles published through 2025, categorized dimensions, including modelling approaches, data, host types, biological levels, spatial scales, temporal scales and model objectives, examined associations among these dimensions, and synthesized author‐stated limitations and recommendations. Statistical and mechanistic models dominated. Model data centred on population dynamics and demography, disease surveillance, host epidemiology and competence, meteorology and land use and land cover. Most studies focused on poultry or wild birds at regional spatial scales, seasonal/annual and multi‐year temporal scales, population or multi‐population levels, and were retrospective. Machine learning and decision‐making models were less common. Immunity, behaviour and life history, community composition, morphology, viral genetics and viral persistence received less attention. Non‐human mammals, individual and community biological levels, local and broader spatial scales, daily temporal scales and prospective modelling were also less frequently modelled. The authors frequently reported limitations related to data availability, surveillance sampling and reporting bias, and model simplification, while commonly recommending improved data quality and greater model complexity and realism. Future studies can align and integrate modelling approaches, data and structures around clearly defined transmission processes, while accounting for uncertainty and keeping model complexity commensurate with empirical evidence. Priorities include model‐guided surveillance that accounts for imperfect detection, broader integration of understudied hosts and transmission processes, more prospective modelling and expanded applications of machine learning and decision‐making where appropriate. Questions spanning spatiotemporal scales and biological levels may require multi‐scale and multi‐level integration through agent‐based or individual‐based models, complemented with hierarchical Bayesian inference, or linked modules designed around shared objectives.

items.title: Incorporating reef condition into conservation planning to meet place‐based biodiversity outcomes under the Global Biodiversity Framework
items.abstract: To achieve Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) Target 3, the selection of protected areas must consider the condition of ecosystems at sites in addition to the GBF 30% area target. Implementing this consideration for coral reef ecosystems is challenging because data describing condition are patchy and limited. Thus, there is uncertainty in how effective coral reef condition data are for informing conservation priorities. To address this uncertainty, we evaluated whether including ecosystem condition data changed conservation priorities when the objective was to protect reefs and implement Target 3. We tested multiple static and modeled temporal coral reef condition datasets for the Great Barrier Reef and found that including reef condition significantly altered spatial planning priorities (p < 0.001), with effects varying according to the condition indicator used. Almost half of the reefs prioritized for protection when condition metrics were included became low priority when they were excluded. Ignoring information about condition missed conservation targets for ∼22% of reef habitats once condition measures were included, highlighting how presence-only approaches can overestimate conservation benefits by treating lower-condition reefs as equal contributors to biodiversity protection. These differences in priority areas highlight the need to develop and use effective condition metrics for designing marine protected area systems for coral reefs globally. Making such data available and usable for managers and practitioners is a priority for coral reef conservation.

items.title: Plant species' distribution patterns, functional traits, and range shifts along an elevation gradient
items.abstract: Knowledge about species' distributions is essential for understanding biodiversity patterns and predicting responses to climate change. The shapes of species' density distributions reflect how their performance varies across their range – shaped by environment, biotic interactions, and dispersal. Because these distributions reflect emergent properties of populations, they may reveal deterministic processes underlying species' past and future ranges and range shifts. Yet, distribution shape parameters (DSPs) are rarely considered in this context, leaving their potential largely unexplored. We addressed this gap by asking: 1) How do DSPs vary and covary among mountain plant species? 2) How are DSPs related to plant functional traits? 3) Can DSPs and functional traits explain recent range shifts? We quantified DSPs for 283 species across 626 plots spanning a 2000‐m elevation gradient on the Calanda massif, Graubünden, Switzerland, extracted functional traits from the TRY database, and compared DSPs and functional traits to range‐shift rates from two complementary data sources. We found that observed range shapes formed a subset of all possible shapes, suggesting trade‐offs in the drivers of distribution shapes. For example, we found that species abundant at higher elevations had shorter upslope and longer downslope distribution tails, consistent with abiotic stress limitation. Range limits and optima were also correlated with functional traits and distribution skew with species' dispersal distance. Finally, both distribution shapes and functional traits correlated with ongoing range shifts – DSPs outperformed functional traits, but considering both provided greater explanatory power. Overall, our results demonstrate that DSPs offer promising directions for future research into the factors influencing range shifts and our ability to predict them. Specifically, the drivers of DSPs and the relevant temporal scales over which they operate should be explored, potentially providing further insights into species' range shifts.

items.title: Beta diversity analysis reveals high turnover in benthic assemblages between tropical coral and subtropical rocky reefs
items.abstract: Understanding species distributions and biodiversity patterns is an old challenge in ecology and biogeography. This approach is especially important because of the current increase in anthropogenic pressure on coastal ecosystems. The Brazilian coastline is a mosaic of complex marine habitats, including extensive rocky shores and the largest coral reef formation in the Atlantic. By decomposing beta diversity into nestedness and turnover components, we investigated how benthic assemblages are structured and how species composition changes along the transitional zone between rocky and coral reefs. To assess the spatial components of alpha diversity, we also analyzed how species richness varies between neighboring habitats. The pairwise comparison of beta diversity revealed the highest turnover rates between the southern and northern assemblages, suggesting differentiation between the two bioprovinces. Southern provinces were characterized by suspension feeders, whereas northern provinces were dominated by stony corals along a north‒south diversity gradient. Redundancy analysis indicated that temperature was the most important environmental driver shaping benthic composition and distribution. Based on these results, we recognize different diversity patterns among two provinces and detect different levels of vulnerability should a stochastic event occur. Considering that human interference tends to increase in this area, the use of beta diversity partitioning can be a useful analytical tool to recognize communities with different levels of priority for monitoring and establishing conservation efforts.
